previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with HCV- and alcohol-related cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma s/p TACE and recent RFA, and chronic depression presented with diffuse abdominal pain and nausea. She reported poor pain control despite IV hydromorphone and requested trazodone and zolpidem. Evaluation revealed no acute surgical or infectious cause; labs were stable, ultrasound showed a cirrhotic liver without ascites or focal lesion, and KUB demonstrated stool-filled colon. Pain was attributed to constipation, and lactulose was increased. She declined narcotics and sedatives due to liver disease risks. By morning, she reported improvement and readiness for discharge. She was discharged home with continued home medications, ondansetron for nausea, and follow-up plans with her liver and primary care teams. Social work was involved due to significant psychosocial stressors.

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ is a ___ female with diabetes, cirrhosis 
from HCV and alcohol, and depression who presented to the 
hospital with hyperglycemia (BS 802). She was admitted to the 
intensive care unit and got and insulin drip. She was then 
transitioned to the floor on subcutaneous insulin. She will 
continue on insulin after discharge and will follow up with 
___ and ___ primary care physician.

# Hyperglycemia: Likely secondary to HHS (Hyperglycemic 
Hyperosmolar Syndrome) given the patient's history of T2DM. 
Review of records indicates that she had had HgbA1c as high as 
7.6 in ___ and has previously been on glyburide; she was 
on lantus insulin in ___, but has not been on insulin for over 
___ year. Most recent HgbA1c was 5.3 in ___. Given 2L 
NS and started on insulin gtt in the ED, with improvement in 
blood sugar from 803 to 568 on arrival to the MICU. Insulin gtt 
was continued in the MICU until blood sugars were <300, at which 
time she was transitioned to long-acting insulin. She was seen 
by ___ diabetes consultants, who assisted in titrating her 
insulin.  She was discharged on Glargine 25 U QHS, Humalog 8 U 
TID with meals and an ISS.  She will follow up with ___ in 
clinic on ___.

# Abdominal Pain: The pt has chronic abdominal pain and her pain 
may have been worsened by HHS.  She was treated symptomatically 
for her abdominal pain and had a CT abdomen-pelvis that was 
reassuring.

# Hepatitis C/Alcoholic Cirrhosis: Pt's LFTs remained at 
baseline throughout hospitalization.  She remained on her 
outpatient medication regimen. 

# Hematochezia: Small volume hematochezia, likely secondary to 
hemorrhoidal bleed. Initial lactate raised concern for 
intrabdominal pathology such as mesenteric ischemia, but benign 
abdominal exam, benign CT A/P, and normalization of lactate was 
reassuring.  The pt had no hematochezia during her course on the 
medical floor.

# Acute Kidney Injury: Pt had a creatinine of 1.3 on admission.  
This improved to 0.9 with fluids in the ICU and remained at 
baseline for the rest of her hospital course.

# Pancytopenia: Near baseline values, but more marked 
thrombocytopenia with plts 37. Likely secondary to underlying 
liver disease. 

# OSA:  Continued CPAP at night  

# Depression: Continued home antidepressants    

# Alcohol Abuse: She denied recent use, although did admit to 
taking a ""sip"" a few weeks ago in the setting of psychosocial 
stress from her daughter's breast cancer.  Her urine and serum 
toxicology screens were negative.  She relates that she is 
committed to avoiding alcohol use.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  History: ___ with abd pain, chills  // PNA?

TECHNIQUE:  Frontal view of chest

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph ___

FINDINGS: 

Linear opacities in bilateral lung bases are similar to before and likely
chronic atelectasis.  There is no pleural effusion or pneumothorax. 
Cardiomediastinal and hilar silhouettes are normal size.

IMPRESSION: 

No radiographic evidence of pneumonia.

EXAMINATION:  CT abdomen and pelvis

INDICATION:  ___ woman with nausea, vomiting, right abdominal pain,
and cough.  Evaluate for pneumonia and small bowel obstruction.

TECHNIQUE:  Single phase split bolus contrast: MDCT axial images were acquired
through the abdomen and pelvis following intravenous contrast administration
with split bolus technique.
Oral contrast was administered.
Coronal and sagittal reformations were performed and reviewed on PACS.

DOSE:  Acquisition sequence:
   1) Stationary Acquisition 6.5 s, 0.5 cm; CTDIvol = 31.3 mGy (Body) DLP =
15.6 mGy-cm.
   2) Spiral Acquisition 4.6 s, 50.5 cm; CTDIvol = 15.7 mGy (Body) DLP = 792.0
mGy-cm.
 Total DLP (Body) = 808 mGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen and pelvis dated ___.

FINDINGS: 

LOWER CHEST:  Linear, bilateral opacities are overall unchanged from the prior
exam, likely scarring.  Otherwise, bilateral areas of atelectasis are noted. 
No evidence of a pleural or pericardial effusion.

ABDOMEN:

HEPATOBILIARY:  The contour of the liver remains nodular, consistent with
known cirrhosis.  Peripheral, 3.5 x 2.5-cm hypodensity in the periphery of the
left hepatic lobe corresponds to an area of prior ablation, unchanged in size
where previously measured 3.7 x 2.3 cm (series 2, image 14).  No evidence of a
new focal hepatic lesion.  No evidence of intrahepatic biliary ductal
dilation.  The common bile duct remains dilated up to 11 mm, unchanged (series
2, image 26).  There is recanalization of the umbilical vein with extensive
anterior abdominal wall varices, overall unchanged extent (series 2, image
21).  The main portal vein, left, and right portal veins appear patent.  The
splenic vein appears patent.  The SMV also appears patent.  The gallbladder is
not visualized.

PANCREAS: The pancreas has normal attenuation throughout, without evidence of
focal lesions or pancreatic ductal dilatation.  There is no peripancreatic
stranding.

SPLEEN: The spleen shows normal size and attenuation throughout, without
evidence of focal lesions.

ADRENALS: The right and left adrenal glands are normal in size and shape.

URINARY: The kidneys are of normal and symmetric size with normal nephrogram. 
Bilateral renal cortical hypodensities are too small to accurately
characterize on CT but statistically most likely cysts, unchanged.  There is
no evidence of focal renal lesions or hydronephrosis.  There is no perinephric
abnormality.

GASTROINTESTINAL:  Fat density within the wall of the distal esophagus could
suggest sequelae of chronic inflammation (series 2, image 8).  The stomach is
unremarkable.  Small bowel loops demonstrate normal caliber, wall thickness,
and enhancement throughout.  The colon and rectum are within normal limits. 
The appendix has a small stone or barium without evidence of acute
appendicitis (series 2, image 51).

PELVIS: The urinary bladder is decompressed with a Foley catheter in place and
balloon inflated.  The distal ureters are unremarkable.  There is a small
amount of free fluid in the pelvis (series 2, image 64; series 602b, image
44).  A small 3.3 x 2.7 cm predominantly hypodense fluid collection anterior
and inferior to the urinary bladder with focal areas of hyperdensity
corresponding to likely calcification are unchanged from the prior exam,
thought to reflect a hematoma in the setting of prior trauma, overall
unchanged (series 2, image 75; series 601b, image 41).

REPRODUCTIVE ORGANS: The uterus and adnexal regions appear grossly within
normal limits.  Uterus is retroverted.

LYMPH NODES:  A 2.1 x 1.6-cm lymph node in the gastrohepatic ligament is
unchanged, likely reactive in the setting of known cirrhosis (series 2 CT
image 20).  Other prominent lymph nodes in the porta hepaticus and hilum of
the liver are unchanged.  No pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

VASCULAR: No abdominal aortic aneurysm.  Moderate atherosclerotic disease is
noted.

BONES: There is no evidence of worrisome osseous lesions or acute fracture. 
Chronic, displaced left superior and inferior pubic rami fractures are again
seen (series 2, image 74, 79).  Sclerosis in the bilateral sacral ala are also
noted again seen, compatible with old fractures.

SOFT TISSUES: The abdominal and pelvic wall is within normal limits other than
venous collaterals.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  No pneumonia.  Bilateral segmental atelectasis and/or scarring.

2.  No bowel obstruction.

3.  Cirrhosis and sequela with unchanged appearance of left hepatic lobe
ablation bed.  Patent main portal vein.

4.  Prominent common bile duct, measuring up to 11 mm, unchanged, likely
related to history of cholecystectomy.

5.  Old pelvic fractures and unchanged appearance of a probable chronic
hematoma related to prior trauma anterior and inferior to the urinary bladder.
